summary: Johann II Bernoulli studied at the University of Basel from around 1723 to 1729. He later taught Johann III Bernoulli and held a post at the University of Basel from circa 1743 to 1790.

Johann III Bernoulli studied at the University of Neuchâtel and the University of Basel under Johann II Bernoulli and Daniel Bernoulli. A scholar in Indology and history/archaeology, he held appointments at the Berlin Observatory and the Prussian Academy of Sciences.
Johann Jakob Engel was a philosopher who studied at the University of Rostock (~1759–1762) and the University of Leipzig (~1762–1765). He later taught Wilhelm von Humboldt.

Indologist Johann Jakob Meyer studied at Concordia Senior College, Concordia Seminary, and the University of Chicago under Carl Darling Buck, earning his Ph.D. in 1900. He served as a docent at the University of Chicago from 1908 to 1919.

Johann Kirste worked in Indology and linguistics, studying at Graz, Berlin, Jena, Leipzig, Vienna (Ph.D.), and Paris under scholars including Georg Bóhler. He held posts at the University of Vienna (1886) and the University of Graz (1892–1902).

Johann Peter Rottler worked in Indology and linguistics after studying at the University of Strasbourg (~1772–1775). He held posts with the Danish-Halle Mission, Tranquebar Botanical Garden, Female Orphan Asylum, and Vepery Mission.

Working in linguistics and Indology, Johann Philipp Fabricius studied law at the University of Giessen (~1732–1735) and theology at the University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1735–1739). In 1742, he succeeded Benjamin Schultze.

Johann Reinhold Forster studied at the Joachimsthalsches Gymnasium and the University of Halle-Wittenberg (1753–1765). In 1780, he was appointed Professor of Natural History at the University of Halle-Wittenberg.

Johann Tobias Beck was a religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Tübingen (~1822–1826). He later held academic posts at the University of Basel (~1836–1843) and the University of Tübingen (~1843–1878).

Johann Wilhelm Andreas Pfaff, who worked in Indology, studied at the University of Tübingen (~1793–1797). He held posts at the University of Tartu (~1803–1809), University of Würzburg (~1814–1818), and University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1818–1835).

Johanna Engelberta van Lohuizen-de Leeuw studied at Leiden and Utrecht under Jan Gonda and others. Specializing in Indology and history/archaeology, she taught at Utrecht and Groningen before serving at Cambridge and the University of Amsterdam.

Johanna Narten studied at Saarland University and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg under Karl Hoffmann and Ernst Zinn. Specializing in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies, she served as an assistant at Erlangen-Nuremberg (1973–1977).

Johannes Baunack, an Indologist and linguist, earned his Ph.D. at the University of Leipzig under Georg Curtius, also studying under Adalbert Kuhn, Friedrich Zarncke, and Hermann Brockhaus. He later served as an Oberlehrer at Alte Nikolaischule (1880–1900).

Johannes Beltz works in Indology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Halle-Wittenberg, Lausanne, and EPHE under Marie-Louise Reiniche and Johannes Bronkhorst, and held posts at Heidelberg University (1996–2001) and Museum Rietberg (2001).

Johannes Bronkhorst, specializing in Indology, Buddhist studies, and philosophy, studied at VU Amsterdam, Rajasthan, Pune (Ph.D. under S. D. Joshi), and Leiden. He held posts at the Kern Institute, Leiden, and the University of Lausanne (1987–2025).
Johannes Brune worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Kiel University from 1903 to 1909, earning a Ph.D. while studying under Hermann Oldenberg and Paul Deussen.

Johannes Edvard Lehmann studied at Copenhagen and Leiden under Fausbøll and Tiele. Specializing in religious studies and Iranian/Central Asian studies, he held academic posts at Copenhagen (1896–1910), Humboldt University of Berlin (1910–1913), and Lund University (1913–1928).

Johannes Friedrich worked in linguistics and history/archaeology. After studying at the University of Leipzig (~1911–1918), he held posts at the University of Leipzig (~1924–1950) and the Free University of Berlin (~1950–1961).

Johannes Gijsbertus de Casparis was an Indologist and historian/archaeologist who studied at Leiden University (~1934–1939). He later served at SOAS University of London (~1957–1986) and as a professor at Leiden University (1978–1986).
Johannes Haeberlin was an Indologist who studied at the Basel Mission Seminary in 1827 and at the Church Missionary Society College, Islington, in 1830.
